summary: A target-level continuation of the accepted DY.3 plan: regular projective dynatomic models and cyclic quotients, explicit quadratic genus and infinity-place formulas, the quadratic-differential and kneading inputs to smoothness and irreducibility, Morton’s explicit two-3-cycle reduction, and certified number-field enumeration adapters. Existing period multiplicity theory, height bounds, filters and arithmetic exclusions retain their parent ids. Analytic source/comparison gaps and supplier rank hypotheses are exposed rather than treated as formalized facts.

nodes.title: Smooth projective models of marked dynatomic curves
nodes.statement: For d≥2,n≥1 and a characteristic-zero field k, put A=k[c,x]/(Φ*ₙ,d), using the inherited monic dynatomic polynomial. Once geometric integrality of A is established, F=Frac(A) is a one-variable function field with exact constants k. Define X₁,d(n) as the regular projective model of F supplied by AlgebraicCurves, with the open immersion Y₁,d(n)→X₁,d(n) from the smooth affine model. The element c∈F induces a finite morphism π₁:X₁,d(n)→ℙ¹_k of degree ν_d(n)=Σ_{e|n} μ(n/e)d^e. This is the normalization of the projective closure; the possibly singular plane closure is not the model used for genus or rational points.
hypotheses: k a field of characteristic zero; d≥2,n≥1.
Geometric integrality and affine smoothness are discharged by the analytic identification target, not assumed to follow from monicity.
proofSteps: Use the inherited coordinate ring and its geometric-integrality endpoint, refined by analytic-dynatomic-identification below. Monicity makes A finite over k[c].
Use AlgebraicCurves Layers 0,2,12 to form the function field and its unique regular projective model; characteristic zero makes the regular model smooth.
Extend c and x as rational functions on the model; the field inclusion k(c)⊂F gives π₁, of degree deg_x Φ*. Uniqueness of the model gives the normalization and base-change comparisons.

sources.match: Projective normalization, rotation and geometric irreducibility.
Smooth projective X₁(n) as normalization, in characteristic zero.

acceptance: For d=2,n=1, X₁ is ℙ¹ with c=x−x² and π₁ degree2.
At n=5, genus is14, not the arithmetic genus of its degree30 plane closure.

nodes.title: Projective quotient by cycle rotation
nodes.statement: Extend the inherited rotation σ(x)=x^d+c, σ(c)=c to F and its smooth projective model. Its order is exactly n (including order1 at n=1), since a generic marked point has exact period n. Set F₀=F^{⟨σ⟩}; X₀,d(n) is the regular projective model of F₀. The inclusion F₀⊂F gives q:X₁→X₀ of degree n, and π₁ factors uniquely through π₀:X₀→ℙ¹ of degree ν_d(n)/n. On the open subset of exact-period points away from ramification, geometric fibres of q are the n cyclic markings of one cycle. A k-point of X₀ there represents a Galois-stable cycle, which need not have any k-rational marked point.
hypotheses: Characteristic zero field k; d≥2,n≥1.
Use the open exact-period locus for the cycle interpretation; boundary and lower-period points remain in the projective quotient.
proofSteps: The ring automorphism extends to the fraction field; its n-th power is identity. Generic exact period gives order exactly n.
Import AlgebraicCurves Layer11 fixed-field degree theorem and Layer12 dictionary to define the quotient model and finite maps.

Over an algebraic closure, q identifies precisely the rotation orbits; descent of that orbit is Galois stability. A rational lift requires trivial Galois action on the marked points, an additional condition.

nodes.title: Primitive binary necklaces at infinity
nodes.statement: For n≥1, a binary word is w:Fin n→Fin2. It is primitive when no nonidentity rotation fixes it. Let Bₙ be primitive words modulo cyclic rotation. Complement w↦1−w induces an involution on Bₙ; let Iₙ be its orbit set. The separate ramification theorem identifies these finite quotients with the geometric places over c=∞ in X₀,2(n). Write ν(n)=ν₂(n)/2 and eₙ=|Iₙ|. Then |Bₙ|=2ν(n)/n and eₙ=ν(n)/n for odd n; for even n, eₙ=ν(n)/n+(1/(2n))Σ_{r|n,2|r,n/r odd} μ(n/r)2^{r/2}. All divisions in these formulas are rational equalities, followed by integrality theorems.
hypotheses: n≥1; binary words have labelled positions before quotienting.
Primitivity excludes all proper cyclic periods, not only constant words.
proofSteps: Use finite cyclic group rotation on Fin n and its action on functions; define primitive words by stabilizer triviality. Complement commutes with rotation.
Möbius inversion counts primitive words. Burnside on rotations and complement counts Iₙ; rotations paired with complement contribute only in the even case with the displayed parity restriction.
Morton Lemma12 identifies these complement-orbits with places at infinity after adjoining u with c=u²; the sign change u↦−u exchanges binary symbols.

nodes.title: Ramification of the quadratic parameter maps
nodes.statement: Over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, put ν(n)=½Σ_{e|n}μ(n/e)2^e. For X₁(n)→ℙ¹_c the degree is2ν(n); above∞ there are ν(n) places each of index2. The finite branch parameters partition into primitive period-n parabolic parameters (bₙ of them) and satellite parameters of exact cycle period e<n with multiplier of order n/e (b_{n,e} of them). Here b_{n,e}=ν(e)φ(n/e) and bₙ=ν(n)−Σ_{e|n,e<n}b_{n,e}. Each primitive parameter has n ramified places of index2; each satellite parameter has e places of index n/e; all other places above those parameters are unramified. Consequently deg Diff(F/k(c))=nν(n)−Σ_{e|n,e<n}eν(e)φ(n/e)+ν(n). For F₀/k(c), finite different degree is bₙ and infinity different degree is 2ν(n)/n−eₙ.
hypotheses: k algebraically closed, char0; n≥1.
Ramification of the normalized curve is used; the discriminant of a possibly nonnormal multiplier plane equation is not its field different.
proofSteps: Use parabolic-parameter-transversality and the local branch descriptions to count primitive and satellite branch parameters via multiplier/cyclotomic factors.
Morton Proposition9 proves the affine coordinate ring is the integral closure and computes finite different exponents, including the satellite contribution n−e.
At infinity use c=u² and the distinct Laurent expansions of periodic roots (Morton Proposition10); for F₀ use primitive binary necklaces and their complement stabilizers.

Characteristic zero is tame, so import different exponent e−1 from AlgebraicCurves Layer7; sum contributions with residue degree1. The quotient is unramified at satellite parameters, not at primitive ones.

nodes.title: Genus formulas for quadratic dynatomic models
nodes.statement: For every n≥1 over any characteristic-zero field, the smooth projective models of z²+c have genera g₁(n)=1+(n−3)ν(n)/2−½Σ_{e|n,e<n}eν(e)φ(n/e), and g₀(n)=1+(½−3/(2n))ν(n)−½Σ_{e|n,e<n}ν(e)φ(n/e)−ε(n), where ν(n)=½Σ_{e|n}μ(n/e)2^e, ε(n)=0 for odd n, and ε(n)=(1/(4n))Σ_{r|n,2|r,n/r odd}μ(n/r)2^{r/2} for even n. These are equalities in ℚ with the natural-number genus cast into ℚ. For n=1,…,10, the pairs (g₀,g₁) are (0,0),(0,0),(0,0),(0,2),(2,14),(4,34),(16,124),(32,285),(79,745),(162,1690).
hypotheses: n≥1; char0; smooth projective models, not affine curves or singular plane closures.
proofSteps: Base change to an algebraic closure preserves genus by AlgebraicCurves Layer8.
Apply the Hurwitz genus formula to both finite separable parameter maps using quadratic-parameter-ramification and genus0 of ℙ¹.
Insert the necklace formula for eₙ and simplify over ℚ. This also proves integrality and nonnegativity; no truncated natural subtraction is used.

sources.match: Both formulas and numerical checks.

nodes.title: Rational quadratic differentials on the complex plane
nodes.statement: A rational quadratic differential is q(z)dz² with q∈RatFunc ℂ. Its pole orders are those of q on the affine plane; at∞ use w=1/z, giving coefficient q(1/w)/w⁴. For a bounded measurable U⊂ℂ and q with at most simple affine poles, define its local mass ∫_U |q(z)| dA, using Lebesgue area on ℂ≃ℝ² and ignoring finitely many poles. It is finite on bounded sets. The double-pole differentials used for multiplier variation are the same rational carrier but are not assigned a finite mass on sets containing their poles.
hypotheses: q rational; local mass assertions require at most simple affine poles.
Affine local integrability does not imply integrability on the sphere.
proofSteps: Use RatFunc ℂ; polynomial numerator/denominator and multiplicity give pole orders. The dz² notation is a coordinate label, with the stated inversion rule.
Represent evaluation away from poles by numerator/denominator; the arbitrary values at the finite poles do not change the integral.
Near a simple pole use |q(z)|≤C/|z−a| and polar integration; cover the bounded closure by finitely many pole discs and regular compact pieces.

sources.match: Local mass for simple poles and separate double-pole coefficients.

acceptance: ∫_{|z|<R}|1/z|dA=2πR for R>0.
∫_{|z|<R}|1/z²|dA diverges; it is not admitted to the simple-pole mass theorem.

nodes.title: Pushforward of rational quadratic differentials
nodes.statement: For a nonconstant polynomial f over ℂ, define f_*q at regular values z by Σ_{f(w)=z}q(w)/f′(w)², summing distinct preimages; extend this rational function across the finite exceptional set. This gives a ℂ-linear operator RatFunc ℂ→RatFunc ℂ, functorial as (f∘g)_*=f_*∘g_*, with identity pushforward the identity. Simple affine poles stay at most simple; double poles can stay double. For f(z)=z^d+c, d≥2, f_*(1/z)=0 and, for a≠0, f_*(1/(z−a))=(1/f′(a))(1/(z−f(a))−1/(z−c)).
hypotheses: f nonconstant; formulas on regular values first, rational extension second.
The second displayed formula requires a≠0 for the unicritical map.
proofSteps: Form the finite separable extension ℂ(f(z))⊂ℂ(z) and use its trace on q/f′²; identify the target rational coefficient with variable z.
On regular fibres trace equals the displayed finite sum. Extension, linearity and composition follow from rational-function equality and trace transitivity.
At poles use local expansions to bound the pushed pole order. For z^d+c sum over d-th roots to obtain Levin’s formulas.

nodes.title: Local contraction for nonzero simple-pole differentials
nodes.statement: Let f∈ℂ[z] have degree≥2 and q≠0 have at most simple affine poles. There is R>0 such that U=f⁻¹(ball(0,R)) has closure contained in V=ball(0,R), and for every sufficiently large such R, mass(f_*q,V)≤mass(q,U)<mass(q,V). Hence f_*q≠q. The zero differential and degree-one identity are excluded.
hypotheses: Degree f≥2; q≠0; at most simple affine poles.
proofSteps: Polynomial growth of degree≥2 gives a sufficiently large disc with relatively compact preimage.
Away from critical points the complex Jacobian is |f′|²; partition regular fibres and apply area change of variables and the triangle inequality. Exceptional finite sets have measure0.
The annular complement contains a nonempty open set; a nonzero rational coefficient cannot vanish there, giving strict mass loss.

sources.match: Corrected local contraction with the necessary nonzero and degree hypotheses; see E9301.

acceptance: For q=0 both masses are0; strict inequality fails.

nodes.title: Transversality at unicritical parabolic parameters
nodes.statement: For f_c(z)=z^d+c,d≥2, at an exact m-cycle with multiplierρ=1 the derivative ∂_c(f_c^m(z)−z) is nonzero and the cycle has one attracting petal. At an exact m-cycle with primitive r-th-root multiplierρ≠1 (r>1), the implicit continuation ζ(c) exists and its multiplierρ(c) has ρ′(c₀)≠0. For P(c,z)=(f_c^{mr}(z)−z)/(f_c^m(z)−z), polynomial division gives ∂_cP(c₀,z₀)=rρ′(c₀)/(ρ(ρ−1))≠0. Locally the relevant dynatomic branch is a graph c=c(z), with ramification index2 in the first case and r in the second.
hypotheses: d≥2; m≥1; exact m-cycle and specified primitive multiplier.
The one-petal and exact local ramification assertions use the unicritical ray/attracting-basin input recorded separately, not the simple-pole contraction alone.
proofSteps: At multiplier1, form the rational simple-pole differential whose coefficients solve the orbit recurrence; its pushforward difference has the parameter derivative as its sole critical-value coefficient. Local-quadratic-contraction forces that coefficient nonzero.
At ρ≠1, use the implicit function theorem for the m-period equation and differentiate the divided equation to obtain the displayed identity.

For multiplier variation use Q=Σ_k(1/(z−z_k)²+μ_k/(z−z_k)), with μ_{k+1}=μ_k/f′(z_k)−(d−1)/(d z_k^d). Lemma2.8 gives f_*Q−Q=−(ρ′/ρ)/(z−c₀). Lemma2.9 excludes equality by puncturing discs about the cycle and comparing annular masses; double poles cannot use the simple-pole integral theorem.
Use the local parabolic normal form and the unique critical basin to give one petal for primitive parameters and r petals for a multiplier of exact order r; this is the named ray/basin gap G1.

sources.match: Derivative calculation and the distinct double-pole argument.

At(c,z)=(−3/4,−1/2), m=1,r=2, the Φ₂ branch has local projection of index2.

nodes.title: Kneading sequences with a boundary symbol
nodes.statement: Fix d≥2. On T=ℝ/ℤ use τ(θ)=dθ. For θ represented in[0,1), let b_j=(θ+j)/d for0≤j<d. For k≥1, ν_θ(k) is ⋆ if τ^{k−1}(θ)=b_j for some j; it is j+1 if it lies strictly between b_j and b_{j+1} for0≤j<d−1; it is0 on the remaining open circular arc from b_{d−1} to b₀. The value ⋆ belongs to Option(Fin d), distinct from every digit. For θ of exact τ-period n, the first ⋆ is at k=n and the kneading sequence is periodic of length n. A word of length n ending in⋆ is cyclic if it is w^{s−1}w⋆ for a word w of length t<n with n=ts; w⋆ replaces only the final digit by⋆. Its cyclic expression uses the unique primitive such w.
hypotheses: d≥2; normalized representative of θ in[0,1); indices k begin at1.
Circular wrap interval has label0, not d; endpoints have label⋆.
proofSteps: Use AddCircle1 for ℝ/ℤ and its normalized representative; make endpoint tests before open-arc tests.
The nth iterate criterion gives the first boundary visit and period of the sequence.
Primitive word means trivial cyclic-rotation stabilizer; the word-combinatorics node proves uniqueness of the primitive cyclic expression.

nodes.title: Primitive-word facts for kneading monodromy
nodes.statement: Every nonempty finite word has a unique primitive root under concatenation. If a nonprimitive word is changed at exactly its last digit, the resulting word is primitive. A cyclic starred kneading block has a unique primitive cyclic expression. For a τ-periodic angle maximal in its orbit, its kneading block is its periodic base-d expansion with the last digit replaced by⋆.

nodes.title: Böttcher coordinates and unicritical external rays
nodes.statement: For d≥2 let K_c={z: the forward orbit under f_c=z^d+c is bounded}, using the inherited escape-rate/bounded-orbit comparison and M_d={c:0∈K_c}. Construct the normalized Böttcher coordinate near∞, φ_c(f_c(z))=φ_c(z)^d and φ_c(z)/z→1. For c∈M_d extend it to ℂ∖K_c≅ℂ∖closedDisc(0,1). Define dynamical rays as inverse radial half-lines, with landing a radial limit as radius decreases to1; for c∉M_d extend the rays maximally, stopping at a critical preimage if continuation breaks. Construct the parameter coordinate Φ_d(c)=φ_c(c), a biholomorphism ℂ∖M_d→ℂ∖closedDisc(0,1); parameter rays are its inverse radial half-lines. These are actual curves, not names for arbitrary choices of landing functions.

Extend on the escaping basin when K_c is connected; prove parameter uniformization and connectivity of M_d using the critical-value coordinate.

Analytic continuation along rays defines the maximal external ray; continuation ends at a precritical point or lands on K_c. The foundational source-to-baseline proof of these dynamical inputs is gap G1; the general conformal/monodromy theory is imported, not replanned.

nodes.title: Periodic ray landing and unicritical parabolic structure
nodes.statement: For d≥2, every periodic parameter ray of exact angle period n lands at a parabolic parameter c₀. Its dynamic ray lands at an exact m-period point with m|n and multiplier a primitive (n/m)-th root of unity. Each period-n hyperbolic component has one root at which two period-n parameter rays land and d−2 co-roots at which one such ray lands; the root is primitive when the two ray orbits are distinct. An exact m-cycle with primitive r-th-root multiplier has the local splitting into one m-cycle and one mr-cycle described in Gao–Ou Lemma3.9; at primitive multiplier1 a single parabolic cycle splits into two m-cycles. Unicriticality gives the one critical attracting basin and the exact petal count used in transversality. For approaching parameters along a landing ray, For the compactified critical-value ray R, any Hausdorff subsequential limit meets ∂K only at the corresponding parabolic point, agrees outside K with its landing ray, and meets int K only inside that point’s immediate basin. The limit S of the precritical pullbacks is f⁻¹(R), so its boundary intersection lies in the preimages of that point. These are the primitive and distinguished-satellite configurations used by the two monodromy propositions.
hypotheses: d≥2; periodic angles; hyperbolic-component root/co-root assertion for n>1 as used in §3.3.
This target uses gap G1: Gao–Ou recall deep ray and basin inputs rather than proving them; no existing ConformalMapping layer supplies polynomial dynamics.
proofSteps: Prove periodic landing and the multiplier/angle-period relation using Böttcher coordinates, orbit portraits and parabolic local dynamics.
Use the multiplier map of a unicritical hyperbolic component (degree d−1, one branch point) to distinguish its unique root from d−2 co-roots.

Prove the local petal/splitting statement and the stated ray-limit control. Gao–Ou cite Douady–Hubbard, Eberlein and Petersen–Ryd here; a full source-to-library extraction is the remaining gap G1, with the exact required outputs in this statement.

Itinerary gives a bijection ι_c:K_c→(Fin d)^ℕ conjugating f_c to the left shift. Thus exact point period equals exact sequence period. On X=ℂ∖(M_d∪R_{M_d}(0)), the inverse x(ι,c) for a fixed sequence is continuous in c, and for a periodic sequence is holomorphic. This supplies the consistent labels for periodic roots in the monodromy calculation.

Recover the unique itinerary point; show conjugacy and exact period preservation. For periodic itineraries apply the implicit function theorem since their cycles are repelling outside M_d.

nodes.title: Local monodromy on labelled periodic points
nodes.statement: Let θ have exact angle period n≥2 and kneading block ε₁…εₙ₋₁⋆. If its parameter ray lands at a primitive parabolic parameter, a sufficiently small positively oriented loop there exchanges the periodic roots labelled ε₁…εₙ₋₁k and ε₁…εₙ₋₁(k+1), where k is the final base-d digit of θ and labels are read mod d, and makes the corresponding exchanges on their cyclic iterates; other nearby roots are fixed. For θ=1−1/(d^n−1), the landing is satellite with fixed parabolic point and the loop permutes cyclically all n points in the cycle labelled (d−1)…(d−1)(d−2). A satellite landing of a maximal angle has cyclic kneading w^{s−1}w⋆ and final digit w_t−1; its parabolic period is |w|.
hypotheses: d≥2,n≥2; analytic continuation based on the consistent labels from X; loops avoid all other branch parameters.
proofSteps: At a primitive point the local projection is c=c₀+δ²; a turn exchanges its two branches. Ray-limit control identifies the two symbolic labels and their rotations.

At the distinguished satellite point the local projection is c=c₀+δ^n, so the branches cycle. Identify its fixed parabolic point with the maximal-angle orbit using Lemma3.14 and the ray-limit exclusion in Proposition3.15.
Lemma3.11 gives the satellite cyclic-expression constraint; Lemma3.12 constructs primitive landing angles when its digit constraint fails.

nodes.title: Transitivity of unicritical marked-point monodromy
nodes.statement: For d≥2,n≥1, remove from the parameter plane the finite branch parameters of the period-n dynatomic curve. Analytic continuation acts transitively on its generic formal period-n roots (all exact period n there). Consequently the smooth affine dynatomic curve has one connected component and its defining polynomial is irreducible over ℂ[c,x].
hypotheses: Generic parameter away from every branch value; n=1 handled by the explicit graph c=z−z^d.
proofSteps: For n>1 rotate a primitive periodic word to its maximal lexicographic marking. If its maximal angle fails the satellite condition, primitive monodromy raises the last digit.

If it satisfies the satellite condition, use the primitive angles of Lemma3.12 successively to reach a word whose total digit sum increases. The sum is bounded by n(d−1)−1, so the process reaches the distinguished orbit with word(d−1)…(d−1)(d−2).
Use the distinguished satellite loop to connect every marking in that orbit; concatenate and reverse loops to connect any two initial roots.
For a smooth affine plane curve, transitivity gives connectedness and hence irreducibility; use analytic/algebraic comparison gap G2 for this final bridge.

The complex smoothness/irreducibility descends to any characteristic-zero field by the integral-coefficient model and faithful field extension. This refines the inherited smooth-irreducible endpoint with the missing closure-to-equation and descent contracts.

nodes.title: The symmetric curve for two marked 3-cycles
nodes.statement: Define H(t,u)=(t²−1)u³+(t³−2t²−9t+2)u²−9(t²−1)u−(t³−2t²−9t+2) overℚ, and let the affine Morton curve be H=0. It is symmetric in t,u. With ζ=t+u,υ=tu, its equation is υ²(ζ−2)−υ(6ζ+4)−(ζ³−2ζ²−9ζ+2)=0. Define t(c,x)=1+2c+2x+2x² on a marked period3 point. For t²≠1, its inverse is x=(t³+t²−t+7)/(4(t²−1)), c=−(t⁶−2t⁵+11t⁴+20t³+23t²−18t+29)/(16(t²−1)²). The rotation sends t to(t+3)/(1−t), and η(t)=(t³−9t)/(t²−1) is constant on the cycle, with c=−(η²−2η+29)/16.

On ζ≠0,2 this defines the quotient by t↔u; the inverse symmetric coordinates are ζ=2/(X−1), υ=(ζ²Y+3ζ+2)/(ζ−2), with t,u the roots of T²−ζT+υ. On the regular projective models this is the degree2 fixed-field quotient, but the affine point-exclusion proof uses only the guarded formulas. At ζ=0 the H-equation forces υ=−1, and at ζ=2 it forces υ=1; hence these cases have(t,u)=(1,−1),(−1,1), or(1,1).
